newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech Q4 GDP growth seen down but rate cut on hold.
newsitem.headline: Czech Q4 GDP growth seen down but rate cut on hold.

text.p: Czech economic growth should show a continued slowdown in the fourth quarter, but analysts said the central bank's fight against inflation still comes first, and interest rates will remain untouched.
The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) is scheduled to release fourth quarter real GDP figures on Friday.
A Reuters survey of local economists showed growth was expected to ease to about 3.4 percent for the fourth quarter, year-on-year, with full year growth expected at 3.6 percent.

That compares with a rise in 1995 fourth quarter GDP of 5.0 percent year-on-year and a full year 1995 increase of 4.8 percent. GDP growth for the first three quarters of 1996 was 3.6 percent higher than for the same period in 1995.
But the analysts said that even though the central bank's tight monetary policy is restricting the economy, they saw little chance of a loosening in interest rates in the near future.
"I expect the central bank will wait for the next trade figures next week before it would decide on any movement in rates," Pavel Sobisek of Zivnostenska Banka told Reuters.
February trade figures from the CSU are expected on Monday. In January, the trade gap was about 7.2 billion crowns ($246 million) after 1996's shortfall hit a record 160.3 billion crowns.

Last summer, the central bank raised its key discount rate by one percentage point to 10.5 percent and implemented a series of measures including repo rate hikes and raising minimum reserve requirements to choke a burgeoning money supply.

The moves appear to be working, with grwoth in M2 money supply, which measures currency, demand deposits, time and savings deposits, and foreign currency deposits, easing to 7.8 percent in December from 20.2 percent in the same month of 1995.
In addition, inflation has continued its gradual easing, dipping to 7.3 percent year-on-year in February.
Government officials have also indicated that the economy is slowing down, with even Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus admitting full year 1996 GDP growth should be one percent lower than expected.

Klaus also cut his forecast for 1997 GDP growth to more than four percent adding this was a "very fitting result" in a European context. But this was a markedly lower than the 5.4 percent forecast on which the 1997 budget was based.

The Czech economy has enjoyed seven years of demand-led growth as industry imported technology and the population, which has seen its wages rise sharply over the past few years, satisfied its thirst for consumer goods.

However, some economists say industrial output has failed to keep pace with wages, and in fact weakened recently, indicating that investment has not been effective and that industry has not carried out vital restructuring.

"Given the recent bad figures, I expect growth to continue slowing in 1997," said one London-based analyst in the survey. "The government may still be over-estimating the pace of growth of the economy."

Last week, the CSU released figures showing real industrial output contracted 3.9 percent year-on-year in January and that construction output was 18.6 percent lower than a year earlier. At the same time, average industrial wages grew 14.4 percent in nominal terms.

EU External Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan, however, gave the Czech economy a vote of confidence on Thursday, saying it was still fundamentally sound and the government was on the right track despite the recent problems.

"The judgment of the European Union is that, of course, every country has its problems, but the progress the Czech economy has made has been remarkable and it remains fundamentally sound," he said after meeting Klaus.
The Czech Republic is a leading contender to be among the first post-communist members of the European Union.
-- Prague Newsroom, 420-2-2423-0003 ($ = 29.25 Czech Crowns)
